overview.title: 📖 Overview: From Teruma's Rules to the Firstborn's Calendar
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 27a–27b
overview.hebrewSource: אֵיזוֹהִי שָׁנָה שֶׁנִּכְנֶסֶת בַּחֲבֶרְתָּהּ? הֱוֵי אוֹמֵר: שָׁנָה שֶׁל בְּכוֹר
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf finishes the previous discussion of paying Temple workers with sacred gifts by drawing a distinction: an owner may accept payment for choosing which priest receives his teruma, but not for the priestly gifts. A cluster of leniencies specific to teruma grown outside Eretz Yisrael follows, illustrated by a vivid travel story involving Rav Naḥman, Rav Amram, and Rami bar Ḥama on a ferry. The Gemara then returns to the mishna's firstborn law, establishing that a firstborn's 'year' is counted from its own birth rather than the calendar year, and offering two independent derivations — one from Rav, one from the school of Rav — for why an unblemished firstborn may be eaten for two days and the night between them, just like the breast and thigh of a peace offering.

slides.title: 🎁 Owner's Discretion: Teruma vs. Priestly Gifts
slides.subtitle: Why one sacred gift may be 'sold' for the right to choose its recipient, and the other may not
headers: May the Owner Accept Payment to Direct It?
rows: It has inherent sanctity (קְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף) and can never be redeemed — no one will mistake it for ordinary food, even after payment changes hands
Their sanctity is value-based (קְדוּשַּׁת דָּמִים) — a priest might think he can 'redeem' them for cash and then treat them like non-sacred food

callout.label: Underlying logic:
callout.text: The Gemara distinguishes gifts by how easily their sanctity could be mistaken for something purchasable and mundane.

slides.title: 🌍 Special Leniencies for Teruma Outside Eretz Yisrael
slides.subtitle: Teruma from outside the Land carries a lighter set of restrictions

boxes.title: Nullification & Impurity (Shmuel)
items: Nullified by a mere majority, unlike ordinary teruma's strict 1:100 ratio
May be eaten by a priest even during his own days of ritual impurity

boxes.title: Timing & Scope (Shmuel)
items: One may eat the produce first and separate teruma from what remains afterward
Forbidden only to a priest whose impurity comes from his own body — not from touching a corpse

boxes.title: Practical Application (Ravina)
items: A menstruating woman may separate ḥalla from dough baked outside Israel
It's fed to a pure minor priest, or a token piece is burned and another separated, so the halakha of ḥalla is not forgotten
An adult priest may eat the rest even while impure

callout.label: Contrast:
callout.text: Rava adds that this teruma even avoids the prohibition against paying a priest-helper at the threshing floor with sacred produce.

slides.title: ⛴️ A Boat, a Question, and Two Rejected Leniencies
slides.subtitle: Rav Naḥman, Rav Amram, and Rami bar Ḥama, traveling together

lines.speaker: A Woman
lines.text: May one impure through corpse-contact immerse and then eat teruma from outside Eretz Yisrael?

lines.speaker: R' Naḥman
lines.text: But do we even have sprinkling of the red heifer's ashes? Without it, how would mere immersion help such a person?

lines.speaker: Rami bar Ḥama
lines.text: Let's wait — shouldn't we be concerned for the opinion of the old man, Rav Amram?

lines.speaker: R' Amram (returning)
lines.text: Rav himself said: one impure from a corpse may immerse and eat outside-Israel teruma.

lines.speaker: Gemara's Verdict
lines.text: The halakha does not follow this leniency — nor a similar one, cited by Mar Zutra in Rav Sheshet's name, for one impure from a creeping animal's carcass.

callout.label: Lesson:
callout.text: Even generous leniencies for outside-Israel teruma have limits — corpse impurity remains too severe for immersion alone to resolve.

slides.title: 📅 Whose 'Year' Counts for a Firstborn?
slides.subtitle: Establishing that the firstborn's year runs from its own birth

steps.content: 1️⃣ The mishna's wording implies the firstborn's 'year' is counted from its own birth, not the calendar year
2️⃣ Rav's proof: 'you shall eat it שָׁנָה בְשָׁנָה' (year by year) — read as one year entering another, describing an animal's personal year spanning two calendar years
3️⃣ The school of Rav reads the same phrase differently: 'one day in this year, one day in that' — teaching an unblemished firstborn may be eaten for two days and the night between
4️⃣ Their broader source: all sacrificial animals' ages are counted from birth, derived from 'a lamb in its own year' (Leviticus 12:6) — 'its year,' not the calendar's

callout.label: Two schools, one conclusion:
callout.text: Rav and his own school reach the same practical rulings about timing through independent readings of related verses.

slides.title: 🍖 Two Days and One Night — Two Separate Derivations
slides.subtitle: Why an unblemished firstborn may be eaten like a peace offering
rows: Numbers 18:18: 'their flesh shall be yours, as the breast of waving and as the right thigh'
Directly compares the firstborn's meat to the peace offering's breast and thigh, which Torah permits for two days and a night
Deuteronomy 15:20 ('year by year'), reread as 'one day in this year, one day in that'
Derives the same two-day-one-night period from the firstborn's own verse, without relying on the peace-offering comparison

callout.label: Same outcome, different paths:
callout.text: Both derivations converge on the identical two-day-one-night eating window, but from entirely separate textual routes.

summary.principle: Sacred gifts differ in how easily their sanctity could be mischaracterized, teruma from outside the Land carries deliberately lighter restrictions, and the firstborn's own 'year' and eating window are both anchored in careful readings of the Torah's exact wording.

flowSteps.content: 🎁 An owner may sell the right to direct his teruma, but not the priestly gifts, based on how each gift's sanctity could be misunderstood
🌍 Teruma from outside Eretz Yisrael carries a cluster of genuine leniencies around nullification, impurity, and timing
⛴️ Even so, a leniency permitting immersion alone to resolve corpse impurity is ultimately rejected

columns.content: 📅 A firstborn's 'year' runs from its own birth, not the calendar
🍖 Two independent verses both yield a two-day-one-night eating window

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Every distinction — who may be paid, what counts as impure, how time is measured — traces back to a precise textual source

quiz.q: Why may an owner accept payment for the right to direct his teruma to a chosen priest, but not for the priestly gifts (foreleg, jaw, maw)?
o: Because teruma is worth less money than the priestly gifts
Because teruma has inherent sanctity that can never be redeemed, so no one mistakes it for mundane food, while the priestly gifts have value-based sanctity a priest might think can be 'bought off'
Because priestly gifts may only be given to the Kohen Gadol
There is no real distinction between the two cases
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that teruma's inherent, non-redeemable sanctity prevents confusion, whereas the priestly gifts have sanctity tied to their monetary value, creating a risk the priest might treat them as ordinary once payment is involved.

quiz.q: According to Shmuel, how does teruma from outside Eretz Yisrael differ from ordinary teruma regarding nullification and consumption during impurity?
o: It cannot be nullified at all, and may never be eaten during impurity
It is nullified by a mere majority rather than 1:100, and may be eaten by a priest even during his own days of ritual impurity
It follows identical rules to ordinary teruma in every respect
It may only be eaten by the Kohen Gadol
quiz.e: Shmuel rules that outside-Israel teruma is nullified in any majority (unlike the strict 100:1 ratio for ordinary teruma) and may be eaten by a priest even while he is ritually impure — both leniencies inapplicable to teruma from Eretz Yisrael.

quiz.q: In the boat story, what did Rav Amram report that Rav ruled about one impure from corpse-contact eating outside-Israel teruma, and does the Gemara accept this as halakha?
o: Rav ruled it forbidden, and the Gemara agrees
Rav ruled that such a person may immerse and eat the teruma, but the Gemara concludes the halakha does not follow this leniency
Rav never issued any ruling on this question
The Gemara accepts the ruling without any reservation
quiz.e: Rav Amram reported that Rav permitted immersion alone to allow eating outside-Israel teruma even after corpse impurity, but the Gemara explicitly states that the halakha does not follow this leniency.

quiz.q: According to Rav's derivation from Deuteronomy 15:20 ('שָׁנָה בְשָׁנָה'), how is a firstborn animal's 'year' calculated?
o: From the first day of the Hebrew calendar year
From the animal's own birth date, spanning into the following calendar year
From the day it develops a blemish
From the day it is given to the priest
quiz.e: Rav reads 'year by year' as describing one year entering another, indicating that the firstborn's personal year is counted from its own birth and can span parts of two different calendar years.

quiz.q: According to Rav's own derivation (as opposed to the school of Rav's), why is an unblemished firstborn eaten for two days and one night?
o: Because Deuteronomy 15:20 explicitly states this time period
Because Numbers 18:18 compares the firstborn's flesh to the breast and thigh of a peace offering, which is eaten for two days and a night
Because the firstborn must be eaten before Shabbat begins
There is no source for this ruling according to Rav
quiz.e: Rav derives the two-day-one-night eating period from Numbers 18:18, which compares the firstborn's meat to the peace offering's breast and thigh — a comparison that carries over the peace offering's own two-day-one-night eating window.
